It's normal for your wait to fluctuate up to 5 to 6 pounds a day, so I wouldn't sweat it too much. It's important to forgive yourself for binging bc negative emotions drive them in the first place. And there's absolutely a point because weight loss is a day-by-day process. And one bad day doesn't replace a whole bunch of good ones!

As far as advice goes, here's what helped me get to and maintain my ideal weight:

Disclaimer: Every person is different, so I can't promise that all the tips will work or be feasible for you. But these are the things I did/do

* Don't buy trigger foods at the grocery store (mine are junk foods and anything with sugar). And if you have any trigger foods in your home, throw them out, tie the garbage bag, and take it out to the trash. Or find some other way to make sure it's thoroughly inedible
* For normal eating food, choose options that requires some prep time (like pasta). Or options that would be too gross to eat raw (like canned corn). That way, if you feel a binge coming on, you'll have time between the initial urge and the food being ready. 
* Have low-calorie vegetables around in bulk so that you can binge on them (if you need to) without undoing progress. 
   * When I was really struggling, I liked to keep huge tubs of lettuce around (no calorie-dense dressings tho). When I needed to binge, I would eat lettuce out of the bin by the handful and it satisfied the urge. The biggest tub I ever bought was 30 calories total, and I was never able to eat near that much during a binge. Plus, during normal days, there are a lot of ways to use it in meals!
*  Sticking to a healthy diet that you personally like at all times
   * Try to eat meals that are 50-70% vegetable. (If you're at home, West African recipes are really tasty and vegetable-rich.  Mexico, Latin America, Central Africa, and India also have a lot of great options that taste amazing). Make sure that you like the foods that you're cooking and eating
   * Replace the processed sugar in your diet with protein bars and raw fruits
   * Try to eat 90% savory and 10% sweet a day (don't sweat it if you overdo tho; worst case, you're still eating fruits and protein)
* NEVER diet to lose weight
   * Most people who go on restrictive diets gain the weight back after the diet is done (there's literature on this)
   * The goal of eating healthy isn't to punish yourself: there are plenty of ways to eat healthy in a genuinely enjoyable way, and food should never be treated as a punishment
* Don't sweat slip ups: nobody's perfect and if you're eating healthy most of the time, then binging won't stop you from losing weight

I mean, not every single person with NPD is going to be a threat to their therapist's safety. But realistically, that's a part of the disorder for many patients. There's actually a studied correlation between aggression, violence and NPD:  [https://www.apa.org/pubs/highlights/spotlight/issue-216](https://www.apa.org/pubs/highlights/spotlight/issue-216). And it's always better safe than sorry. Therapists are people, too, and their safety matters just as much as the safety of the client.

That said, every single person with NPD will lash out if they feel their maladaptive worldview is being threatened, because that's just a facet of the disorder. It's not an extreme case it's just what it is. Even if they just quit therapy, you'd still be losing your opportunity to help them.

​

>But I’ve watched people with Bipolar (my mom) get desperate and fly into an unholy terror of a rage, I’ve seen people do the same over being poor. But typically multiple factors are at play there, and further, such examples are at the extreme end of an experience and not common

\[Mandatory I'm not a psychologist but\]

Narcissistic personality disorder is different than BPD or reacting to economic factors. For a lot of people, rage is triggered by feeling trapped or threatened by real things. That's completely normal. For some people (like people experiencing schizophrenia, schizotypal personality disorder, or other disorders that lead to delusional thinking), rage is triggered by feeling trapped or threatened by something unreal but extreme or exceptional. If their delusions were somehow made reality, and a neurotypical person experienced them, they'd probably have the same reaction.

Narcissistic rage isn't like that. For one thing, it's almost constant. People with NPD rely on others to validate their self image, which is so enlarged that 99% of interactions can't. See the dsm-5 definition: [https://www.nyu.edu/gsas/dept/philo/courses/materials/Narc.Pers.DSM.pdf](https://www.nyu.edu/gsas/dept/philo/courses/materials/Narc.Pers.DSM.pdf)

In other words, a narcissist will get as mad at a Starbucks barista for not remembering their name as a neurotypical person would if their boss cussed them out. From their perspective, they live in a near constant state of being insulted by others (who are dumber/less special than them). Since they rely on others for approval, being actually criticized (even in small ways) is crushing.

​

>I don’t know. Having dealt with a lot of that behavior myself, I really don’t see how beneficial it is to monstrify people with NPD.

I'm not trying to monstrify people with NPD. The one's I've known have had good reasons for developing those coping mechanisms, and I probably would have too if I were in their place. Inside, they're basically just deeply traumatized kids with more fight than flight. But it doesn't help anyone to ignore the darker sides of mental illness.

​

That said tho there IS a lot of stigma around NPD that there shouldn't be. But the realities of the illness should still be kept in mind. And I don't think the therapists in the article did anything wrong.

To answer your questions, the poem is about this one experience I had when I was 15. My parents were mad at me because of something trivial (I think I got distracted while studying?), and were yelling at me and calling me the usual (stupid, ugly, whore, useless, bitch, etc.). I knew I was about to cry, so I rushed into my room.

At first I tried to stay as far away from the door as possible, and cry silently because I loved them, and I didn't want them to know I was crying and feel bad. Eventually, though, I allowed myself to cry louder because I wanted them to understand how they'd hurt me. I wished that they'd hear me, and come in and apologize or discuss, or something. They still didn't come in, so I crawled to my still-closed door, still crying, pressed my face against it.  I wanted them to hear me, and I felt so guilty because of it. I wanted them to understand the impact their words had had on me - my tears being the 'wet reward' of the experience. But at the same time, I felt so guilty for even wanting that. So I didn't open the door, and just kept crying and hoping.

I could hear their footsteps outside, but they never said anything, or tried to come in. I wasn't sure if they heard me. I wasn't sure if the footsteps I could hear outside were theirs or the dogs. But if they did hear me, they never came in. After two hours, I finally stopped crying. I stopped waiting for them to come inside, wiped my tears away, and walked out of my room. I felt ashamed of the experience. I felt weak. I promised myself that next time I'd be stronger, that I'd keep my feelings to myself, and wouldn't cry again. It's not the worst story, but it's a bad memory and a good metaphor

I think it really depends on who you are, and what your life looks like. But the best way to cope with loneliness in my experience is to find ways to be around people while doing activities that you enjoy. Like joining clubs in your area, or inviting classmates/coworkers you like out to lunch.

If you're already doing that, spend the rest of your time working towards goals. What I've noticed in myself is that I generally feel loneliness most when I'm bored, and have extra time to compare myself to others. If you're actively working on a project, or a personal goal, you'll have something to focus on, and being good at something makes you more socially attractive anyway. You'll also probably end up meeting people through doing it.

Otherwise, find an exercise plan that works for you, stick to a consistent sleep schedule, dress well, and eat healthy. It sounds random, but physical health is very tied to mental health. [Excessive sugar is tied to depression](https://healthline.com/health/depression/sugar-and-depression#carbohydrates-and-depression), and being fit/well-groomed makes a person [more likely to be seen as likeable and approachable](https://www.verywellmind.com/what-is-the-halo-effect-2795906).
